newsitem.title: USA: Robot-rover going to Mars this year.
newsitem.headline: Robot-rover going to Mars this year.

text.p: A six-wheeled robot the size of a large toy truck will head for Mars in December, but no humans are likely to go to the red planet until the second decade of the 21st century, NASA's chief said on Wednesday.

The robot, called Sojourner, is meant to function as a mechanical geologist, looking at the terrain and sending back pictures as part of an ambitious 10-mission programme previewed at a briefing by Dan Goldin, head of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

Such pre-flight briefings are typical for NASA, but Goldin's presence is not. He unveiled the first evidence of possible microscopic life on Mars at such an event two months ago, but in Wednesday's appearance he discounted any hopes of a quick human trip to the planet.
"We shouldn't be sending people until we do some reconnaissance with robots," Goldin told reporters.

"I don't think a robot has the dexterity or the ability to reason like a human has, but it's unreasonable to just say, let's go send a human to Mars and feel good when the nation has a whole variety of financial issues to face up to."

Goldin said in response to questions that if a host of techinical and fiscal questions can be answered within the next decade, "I think we could be on Mars (with a human mission) ... in the second decade of the next century."

He said NASA has made no changes in its plans to study Mars since the August announcement that scientists had found evidence of possible microscopic fossilized life-forms that might have come from Mars in a meteorite found in Antarctica.

One way to confirm that the meteorite came from Mars is to bring back similar samples of Martian rock with the same kinds of fossils, and Goldin said the earliest that samples might be recovered would be in the year 2003.

Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun and Earth's next-door neighbour, is widely viewed as the planet most likely to support eventual human expeditions. Mars has all the ingredients necessary for life, including an atmosphere, polar caps and large amounts of water locked beneath its surface.

Goldin heralded the upcoming December 2 launch of the Sojourner robot-rover, which will take pictures of the Martian surface and analyse what it "sees". It should arrive on Mars on July 4, 1997, he said.
Cameras on the Sojourner will beam images back to Earth that will be available on the Internet within 20 to 40 minutes of being snapped on Mars.

Sojourner will be the third in an ambitious decade-long series of 10 flights toward Mars. The first is the Mars Global Surveyor, a satellite about the size of a small bus that is meant to orbit Mars and chart the planet's surface.
It is set to launch November 6, arrive on September 11, 1997, and start its primary mission on March 15, 1998.
The second Mars mission, a Russian orbiter, will be launched from Russia on November 16.
Sojourner will fly to Mars aboard the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft, which will parachute down through the Martian atmosphere and cushion its landing with airbags.

The total programme has three objectives, NASA said: to search for evidence of past life on Mars; to understand the Martian climate with a view to any applicable lessons for Earth's climate; and to understand the geology and resources that could be used to support future human missions to Mars.
Goldin said these new missions to Mars were the first U.S. return to the planet in 20 years.
